值得閱讀的理由

  • 以低生育率與高齡化說明，社會安全網面臨的不只是人口變化，更是財政與制度的考驗。
  • 從世代正義切入退休制度，呈現年輕世代與退休世代之間難以迴避的資源分配問題。
  • 探討非典型勞動者與平台工作者如何落在保障網之外，讓讀者看見勞動型態轉變帶來的風險。
  • 指出福利制度改革不能只轉移帳單，並呼籲以制度改革和公民教育共同打造更公平、可持續的未來。

摘要

社會安全網還撐得住嗎？

阿牛從高房價、低薪與非典型工作者的生活壓力談起，也提醒觀眾，年輕世代如今負擔著逐年增加的保費，支撐上一代退休生活；等到自己三、四十年後老去，國庫是否還有能力承擔，仍是未知數。他指出，若政府無法以社會投資的角度改革制度、要求獲利的平台業者承擔社會責任，並勇於推動真正的退休制度改革，最終可能沒有人能置身事外。

在節目宣傳中，阿牛表示，社會除了需要現金補助，也需要普及的公民教育。系列內容依據教育部一○八課綱的公民與社會領域設計，希望讓基礎公民知識更容易理解，並透過制度改革與公民教育，為重塑社會盡一份心力。接著，他說明本集將討論社會安全網的五項課題：少子化與高齡化、世代公平、非典型勞動、平台經濟，以及財政永續。安全網能否發揮作用，關鍵不只是網有多大，也在於網上有多少破洞。

少子化、高齡化與逐漸變重的負擔

阿牛先以「幾個人撐網、幾個人躺在網上」作比喻：當支撐安全網的人變少、需要依靠它的人變多，網就可能無法承受。國民年金與保險制度多採隨收隨付的方式，也就是由現在的工作者負擔目前退休者的給付，而非每個人都只靠自己的儲蓄。當人口結構從年輕人多、長者少的金字塔，轉為繳費者減少、領取給付者增加的倒金字塔，制度便會承受愈來愈大的壓力。

阿牛引用社會學者阿恩・卡勒伯格對不穩定生活的觀察，指出許多年輕人難以找到穩定工作，也難以規劃人生；買房、結婚與生育等重要選擇只得一再延後。這不是年輕人不夠努力，而是整體結構讓他們進退兩難。學校學生減少、教室合併，甚至校園空間可能改作長者日照用途，也映照出服務對象從孩童轉向長者的人口變化。

戰後嬰兒潮世代陸續退休，使繳納年金與健保的人數逐年減少；另一方面，退休給付、長者醫療資源與長照支出不斷增加。保費負擔愈重，年輕人愈不敢生育，人口與財務壓力也就進一步加劇。阿牛將社會由人口紅利期走向少子高齡期的變化，描述為一個可能持續惡化的惡性循環。

世代契約與公平分擔

阿牛進一步談到世代契約：年輕時照顧上一代，盼望未來由下一代接手照顧自己。然而，這份沒有白紙黑字的契約若失去信任，社會也可能因此分裂。當代享有的福利，有一部分等於預支了未來世代尚未賺取的資源，因此問題不只是要不要照顧長者，更包括由誰承擔成本、如何分配責任。

他援引托馬斯・皮凱提關於資本累積速度快於薪資成長的分析，提出疑問：如果年輕人必須繳更多保費，去支撐資產累積可能已勝過自己的退休世代，這樣的安排是否公平？民主制度也有結構性的時間偏差：現在能投票的人有聲音，尚未出生的世代卻無法參與。以城市預算為例，政府可能選擇立即提高長者福利，而把青年社會住宅延後興建，因為前者今年就能看見成果，後者則須等待多年。

阿牛認為，臺灣退休金改革的爭議，正是世代契約受考驗的表現。改革無法憑空消除成本，往往只是改變由誰付帳；公開精算報告、接受獨立檢視並容許不同意見，才能讓債務與取捨進入公共討論。沒有爭論，不代表問題不存在，代價只是可能以另一種形式到來。

安全網外的非典型勞動者

阿牛接著指出，還有一群人甚至沒有被納入既有的保障計算。他們出現在道路、倉庫與住家門口，卻常常落在安全網之外。臨時工作、自由接案與外送等零工勞動，具有工時不規律、缺少固定雇主等特徵，也往往伴隨保障不足。安全網上的破洞並非偶然，而是制度如何編織、如何界定保障對象的結果。

他引用勞動經濟學者蓋伊・史坦丁對「無產階級化」的描述：這些工作者的生活中缺少對未來的影子。因為無法確定明天是否有工作，今天投入的勞動與作出的承諾便難以轉化為長期保障。與工業時代能以忠誠換取穩定的勞工相比，這群人承受的不只是收入不確定，也包括生活時間感與未來規劃的瓦解。影片字幕在外送員案例尚未說完時中止。

================================================

Every day, we shoulder high housing prices and low wages, struggling in atypical jobs, while being forced to pay ever-increasing premiums each month to support the previous generation's retirement. But thinking about how it will be our turn to grow old in thirty or forty years, the national treasury might be drained by then. So I have to be clear: if the government cannot overhaul the rules with a social investment perspective, cannot force profitable platform operators to fulfill their social responsibilities, and cannot summon the courage to push for real pension reform...This storm will eventually drag everyone down with. it. Commercial break: A while ago, there was a policy to distribute 10,000 NTD to everyone, but what our society needs more right now is a universal distribution of civics textbooks. This isn't just our lament about social phenomena; it's our expectation for education. We are committed to remaking the Republic, and there are two ways to do that: institutional reform and the popularization of civic education. That is why we launched this basic civic education series to achieve our goal of distributing civics textbooks to all. This series is designed based on the Ministry of Education's 108 Curriculum Guidelines for Civics and Society, hoping to make basic civic education accessible and easy to understand for everyone. If you have the means and. would like to support our work, you can consider clicking "Super Thanks" to give us some support, or join as a member to help us go further on this path. You can also leave a comment, or join our Discord or Telegram groups, and let's work together to make the future better. Hello everyone, I’m A-Niu. We previously discussed how the social safety net is formed. Today, let’s talk about whether our social safety net can still hold up. Many people actually have two misconceptions about social welfare: one is thinking it's charity given by the government to the disadvantaged; the second is the belief that "as long as I work hard enough, I don't need to rely on the government." But honestly, we must face. reality. The risks in modern society are extremely high and cannot be withstood by individual effort alone. The past model of staying at the same company until retirement is crumbling, and the demographic dividend has disappeared. Therefore, the question now is not whether we need welfare, but how to design a fair and sustainable safety net. Today, we will discuss five concepts regarding the problems appearing in this social safety net: low birth rates and an aging population , intergenerational equity, atypical. labor, the platform economy, and fiscal sustainability. A social safety net is just a net; whether it works well depends not on how big it is, but on the size of its holes. First, let's talk about the low birth rate and aging population that everyone has likely heard discussed for a long time. If this safety net is held by four people with only one person lying in the middle, it’s obviously very stable. But if there are fewer people holding the net and more people lying on it, what happens then? Basically, it just.

can't hold up anymore. That is the challenge we are currently facing: a low birth rate and an aging population. Because our national pension and insurance systems operate on a pay-as-you-go basis; simply put, these are not personal savings accounts, but rather current workers paying to support those currently retired. Once the population pyramid collapses, this support model gets stuck. Sociologist Arne Kalleberg observed in "Precarious Life" that young people today cannot find stable jobs in the labor market and cannot even plan the next stage of. their lives. Buying a house, getting married, and having children—these major life milestones can only be postponed again and again. It’s not that young people aren't working hard; it’s that the entire social structure leaves them in a dilemma. Look at how many elementary schools now have so few students that classrooms are being merged, playgrounds are becoming parking lots, and in a few years, they might even be repurposed as senior day care centers. On the same plot of land, the target demographic has shifted from six-year-olds to eighty-year-olds, and this is the reality we are experiencing . The previous population structure was a pyramid with plenty of young adults, so the net could hold. Now, it has. become an inverted pyramid: fewer people pay premiums, while more seniors collect benefits and use medical resources, creating a vicious cycle. Premiums become heavier, young people become even less daring to have children, and the net sinks even further. This is the dilemma of the low birth rate that Taiwan is currently facing. On one hand, the post-war baby boomer generation is retiring one after another, and the number of people paying into pension and health insurance is decreasing year by year. On the other hand, the total amount of pension payouts, the medical resources consumed by the elderly, and the public. expenditure for promoting Long-Term Care 2.0 are all increasing almost exponentially. The young adults paying into the system are fewer, while the elderly who collect and spend the money are more. This transition can be divided into two periods. The first is the traditional demographic dividend period: high fertility rates, shorter lifespans, and a standard pyramid structure where many young adults support few seniors, resulting in sufficient funds and generous payouts, with a labor market dominated by standard employment and easy entry for youth. The second is the period of an. aging and low-birth-rate society: ultra-low fertility, longer lifespans, and an inverted pyramid where a few young adults support a vast elderly population. Funds face bankruptcy crises, premiums are heavy, service industries and non-standard employment expand, young people face low wages and delayed family formation, and fertility rates fall yet another level. This is a vicious cycle; whether or not we can afford to support those on the margins has never been a moral issue, but an economic and political one. We shouldn't pretend the reality doesn't.

exist, because this web is woven by the choices of our generation. We must face a sharper issue: the so-called intergenerational contract. The hope was that we would care for the older generation when we were young, and the next generation would care for us when we grew old, but once this unsigned contract breaks, social trust vanishes. This web is essentially overdrawing the future; as we lie on it, we are spending money that the next generation has yet to earn. Once this unsigned. intergenerational contract snaps, society will inevitably fracture along with it. The structural issue mentioned by sociologist Thomas Piketty in " Capital in the Twenty-First Century" is quite real: capital accumulates much faster than wages grow. If the system then requires young people to pay higher premiums to support a retired generation that has already accumulated more assets than them, is that fair to the youth? Often, this unfairness stems from the structural blind spots of democracy: those who can vote are present, but those not yet born cannot. vote. When governments choose to prioritize immediate senior welfare payouts over social housing that won't be ready for years, they are effectively pushing the financial burden onto the next generation. For example, imagine a city budget meeting considering two proposals: increasing monthly senior welfare by 1,000 or building new social housing for youth. If the city budget only allows for one, the decision will be to raise the senior payout this year and put off the. housing for two years. Their reasoning is clear: one result is visible this year, the other in four years. This is a common structural bias in democracy —voters are present, while the unborn are absent. The controversy over pension reform in Taiwan is a symptom of this broken contract. It was never really about who owes whom money, but about whose threads should be used to weave this social safety net. We must admit that "reform" alone cannot solve. the problem; it just shifts the bill to someone else. The reason pension equity became a public debate in Taiwan is that someone was willing to publish the actuarial reports and bear the risk of being criticized. In contrast, in a system without independent audits, public reports, or dissent, this debate would never even happen. However, the absence of debate does not mean the debt doesn't exist; it just arrives in a different form. Therefore, it’s not.

really about who owes whom, but whose thread should be used to weave this social safety net; the original way won’t solve the problem, it just changes who pays. But speaking of this, there is an even more troublesome issue : there is actually a group of people who aren't even included in this calculation. As mentioned earlier, some aren't even eligible to be part of this account, so who are they? They are on the roads, in warehouses, and even right at your doorstep, but they have already fallen outside of the safety net. In fact, the holes in the net. aren't random; they are decided by those who weave it. We’ve discussed gig labor in previous episodes; simply put, it means irregular working hours and no fixed employer, such as temp work, freelancing, or delivery services —all of which share a severe lack of protection. Labor economist Guy Standing, in "The Precariat: The New Dangerous Class," has a very apt description: "There is no shadow of the future in their lives." This means that because they are unsure if they will. have a job tomorrow, the commitments they make and the labor they put in today have no meaning for the future. Compared to the proletariat of the industrial age who could trade loyalty for security, this "precariat" truly has nothing. It’s not just a matter of income; it’s a collapse of their sense of time. Take a delivery driver, for example; the paper they sign with the platform isn't an employment contract, but a service agreement. What’s the difference? The difference is whether there is anyone to catch you the moment you fall. Economist Kathleen. Thelen, in "Varieties of Liberalization and the New Politics of Social Solidarity," proposes the concept of " dualization," because the current labor market is split in two: "insiders" who enjoy full protection and "outsiders" who are thrown into the market to bear all the risks. The irony is that what determines who you are is not your ability, but where the system draws the line. Suppose a bookstore chain converts all its warehouse staff to temp workers; afterwards, there are two types of people in the same warehouse:. one is the original staff with benefits , annual bonuses, and employer-contributed pensions; the other is the temp staff, doing the exact same work in the exact same spot, yet receiving completely different protections. The most concerning part here isn't actually that the conditions are different, but that although they are in the same space, it is difficult to form a sense of "us." We must acknowledge that those who have fallen through the holes are not outsiders, so whether a contract says "employment" or "service" sometimes determines a.

person's destiny more than the law itself. So, who exactly is deciding the rules of the game? Who is setting the terms? In fact, this is a problem brought on by the platform economy. Businesses use digital technology, networks, and algorithms to create a model that matches labor supply with consumer demand. The convenience it brings is real, but it can also simultaneously upend labor relations and the social safety net. In "The Fissured Workplace," economist David. Weil warns that by outsourcing work, companies are transforming the employer responsibilities they should be carrying into cold, hard commercial contracts. Wages are no longer pay; they are just pricing. Simply put, platforms have become free riders in the welfare system. As sociologist Juliet Schor noted in "After the Gig," platforms shift the costs of worker health and retirement onto society, while maximizing their own profits through an "asset-light" model that avoids ownership as much as possible. Take delivery drivers as an example: the vehicle is theirs and they pay for the gas, but it is that invisible manager—the algorithm—that decides when they stop and how much they earn per order. When issues arise, the platform just says, "We are merely intermediaries; what we signed were service contracts." And just like that, employer liability vanishes into thin air. Delivery platforms in Taiwan operate roughly this way. Through mobile app algorithms, they unilaterally and opaquely determine each driver's order volume, delivery distance, payment rates per order,. bonus thresholds, and the conditions for suspension. However, when faced with labor inspections or legal disputes, the platform’s stance shifts to: "Drivers are independent contractors; the platform only manages dispatching and ratings, and does not hold the status of an employer." In practice, they manage with an iron fist , yet in name, they bear no responsibility whatsoever. This is exactly the greatest challenge the platform economy poses to traditional labor laws. We can now see that those who manage the most strictly often bear the least responsibility. If this holds. true in reality, it is not because the market is broken, but because the rules were written incorrectly. So, how should we rewrite the rules? Although everyone knows the rules need to change , the most pressing and difficult hurdle to clear is where the money will actually come from. Previously, we were all teaching people how to mend this safety net, but there is actually a more radical approach: weaving the entire net differently. 值得閱讀的理由

  • 以低生育率與高齡化說明，社會安全網面臨的不只是人口變化，更是財政與制度的考驗。
  • 從世代正義切入退休制度，呈現年輕世代與退休世代之間難以迴避的資源分配問題。
  • 探討非典型勞動者與平台工作者如何落在保障網之外，讓讀者看見勞動型態轉變帶來的風險。
  • 指出福利制度改革不能只轉移帳單，並呼籲以制度改革和公民教育共同打造更公平、可持續的未來。

摘要

社會安全網還撐得住嗎？

阿牛從高房價、低薪與非典型工作者的生活壓力談起，也提醒觀眾，年輕世代如今負擔著逐年增加的保費，支撐上一代退休生活；等到自己三、四十年後老去，國庫是否還有能力承擔，仍是未知數。他指出，若政府無法以社會投資的角度改革制度、要求獲利的平台業者承擔社會責任，並勇於推動真正的退休制度改革，最終可能沒有人能置身事外。

在節目宣傳中，阿牛表示，社會除了需要現金補助，也需要普及的公民教育。系列內容依據教育部一○八課綱的公民與社會領域設計，希望讓基礎公民知識更容易理解，並透過制度改革與公民教育，為重塑社會盡一份心力。接著，他說明本集將討論社會安全網的五項課題：少子化與高齡化、世代公平、非典型勞動、平台經濟，以及財政永續。安全網能否發揮作用，關鍵不只是網有多大，也在於網上有多少破洞。

少子化、高齡化與逐漸變重的負擔

阿牛先以「幾個人撐網、幾個人躺在網上」作比喻：當支撐安全網的人變少、需要依靠它的人變多，網就可能無法承受。國民年金與保險制度多採隨收隨付的方式，也就是由現在的工作者負擔目前退休者的給付，而非每個人都只靠自己的儲蓄。當人口結構從年輕人多、長者少的金字塔，轉為繳費者減少、領取給付者增加的倒金字塔，制度便會承受愈來愈大的壓力。

阿牛引用社會學者阿恩・卡勒伯格對不穩定生活的觀察，指出許多年輕人難以找到穩定工作，也難以規劃人生；買房、結婚與生育等重要選擇只得一再延後。這不是年輕人不夠努力，而是整體結構讓他們進退兩難。學校學生減少、教室合併，甚至校園空間可能改作長者日照用途，也映照出服務對象從孩童轉向長者的人口變化。

戰後嬰兒潮世代陸續退休，使繳納年金與健保的人數逐年減少；另一方面，退休給付、長者醫療資源與長照支出不斷增加。保費負擔愈重，年輕人愈不敢生育，人口與財務壓力也就進一步加劇。阿牛將社會由人口紅利期走向少子高齡期的變化，描述為一個可能持續惡化的惡性循環。

世代契約與公平分擔

阿牛進一步談到世代契約：年輕時照顧上一代，盼望未來由下一代接手照顧自己。然而，這份沒有白紙黑字的契約若失去信任，社會也可能因此分裂。當代享有的福利，有一部分等於預支了未來世代尚未賺取的資源，因此問題不只是要不要照顧長者，更包括由誰承擔成本、如何分配責任。

他援引托馬斯・皮凱提關於資本累積速度快於薪資成長的分析，提出疑問：如果年輕人必須繳更多保費，去支撐資產累積可能已勝過自己的退休世代，這樣的安排是否公平？民主制度也有結構性的時間偏差：現在能投票的人有聲音，尚未出生的世代卻無法參與。以城市預算為例，政府可能選擇立即提高長者福利，而把青年社會住宅延後興建，因為前者今年就能看見成果，後者則須等待多年。

阿牛認為，臺灣退休金改革的爭議，正是世代契約受考驗的表現。改革無法憑空消除成本，往往只是改變由誰付帳；公開精算報告、接受獨立檢視並容許不同意見，才能讓債務與取捨進入公共討論。沒有爭論，不代表問題不存在，代價只是可能以另一種形式到來。

安全網外的非典型勞動者

阿牛接著指出，還有一群人甚至沒有被納入既有的保障計算。他們出現在道路、倉庫與住家門口，卻常常落在安全網之外。臨時工作、自由接案與外送等零工勞動，具有工時不規律、缺少固定雇主等特徵，也往往伴隨保障不足。安全網上的破洞並非偶然，而是制度如何編織、如何界定保障對象的結果。

As mentioned earlier, some aren't even eligible to be part of this account, so who are they? They are on the roads, in warehouses, and even right at your doorstep, but they have already fallen outside of the safety net. In fact, the holes in the net. aren't random; they are decided by those who weave it. We’ve discussed gig labor in previous episodes; simply put, it means irregular working hours and no fixed employer, such as temp work, freelancing, or delivery services —all of which share a severe lack of protection. Labor economist Guy Standing, in "The Precariat: The New Dangerous Class," has a very apt description: "There is no shadow of the future in their lives." This means that because they are unsure if they will. have a job tomorrow, the commitments they make and the labor they put in today have no meaning for the future. Compared to the proletariat of the industrial age who could trade loyalty for security, this "precariat" truly has nothing. It’s not just a matter of income; it’s a collapse of their sense of time. Take a delivery driver, for example; the paper they sign with the platform isn't an employment contract, but a service agreement. What’s the difference? The difference is whether there is anyone to catch you the moment you fall. Economist Kathleen. Thelen, in "Varieties of Liberalization and the New Politics of Social Solidarity," proposes the concept of " dualization," because the current labor market is split in two: "insiders" who enjoy full protection and "outsiders" who are thrown into the market to bear all the risks. The irony is that what determines who you are is not your ability, but where the system draws the line. Suppose a bookstore chain converts all its warehouse staff to temp workers; afterwards, there are two types of people in the same warehouse:. one is the original staff with benefits , annual bonuses, and employer-contributed pensions; the other is the temp staff, doing the exact same work in the exact same spot, yet receiving completely different protections. The most concerning part here isn't actually that the conditions are different, but that although they are in the same space, it is difficult to form a sense of "us." We must acknowledge that those who have fallen through the holes are not outsiders, so whether a contract says "employment" or "service" sometimes determines a.

person's destiny more than the law itself. So, who exactly is deciding the rules of the game? Who is setting the terms? In fact, this is a problem brought on by the platform economy. Businesses use digital technology, networks, and algorithms to create a model that matches labor supply with consumer demand. The convenience it brings is real, but it can also simultaneously upend labor relations and the social safety net. In "The Fissured Workplace," economist David. Weil warns that by outsourcing work, companies are transforming the employer responsibilities they should be carrying into cold, hard commercial contracts. Wages are no longer pay; they are just pricing. Simply put, platforms have become free riders in the welfare system. As sociologist Juliet Schor noted in "After the Gig," platforms shift the costs of worker health and retirement onto society, while maximizing their own profits through an "asset-light" model that avoids ownership as much as possible. Take delivery drivers as an example: the vehicle is theirs and they pay for the gas, but it is that invisible manager—the algorithm—that decides when they stop and how much they earn per order. When issues arise, the platform just says, "We are merely intermediaries; what we signed were service contracts." And just like that, employer liability vanishes into thin air. Delivery platforms in Taiwan operate roughly this way. Through mobile app algorithms, they unilaterally and opaquely determine each driver's order volume, delivery distance, payment rates per order,. bonus thresholds, and the conditions for suspension. However, when faced with labor inspections or legal disputes, the platform’s stance shifts to: "Drivers are independent contractors; the platform only manages dispatching and ratings, and does not hold the status of an employer." In practice, they manage with an iron fist , yet in name, they bear no responsibility whatsoever. This is exactly the greatest challenge the platform economy poses to traditional labor laws. We can now see that those who manage the most strictly often bear the least responsibility. If this holds. true in reality, it is not because the market is broken, but because the rules were written incorrectly. So, how should we rewrite the rules? Although everyone knows the rules need to change , the most pressing and difficult hurdle to clear is where the money will actually come from. Previously, we were all teaching people how to mend this safety net, but there is actually a more radical approach: weaving the entire net differently. With limited national resources, the government must strike a balance between fairness, efficiency, funding, and political.

reality—this is what we call fiscal sustainability. When many people hear " fiscal sustainability," they immediately think of cutting spending, slashing budgets, and reducing welfare, but they are completely missing the point. French sociologist Guillaume Morel once proposed a sound principle: preparation beforehand is better than repairs afterward. In other words, rather than waiting for someone to fall from a building half-dead and scrambling to catch them with a net, it is better to build a railing or raise the ground beneath their feet from the very start. When we view social welfare. not as mere consumption, but as an investment that yields returns, the entire calculation changes completely. Looking back at history, traditional post-war Western welfare states favored passive, reactive compensation— providing relief for the unemployed and pensions for the elderly. This worked well in an era of rapid economic growth when the youth population outnumbered the elderly. But by the 1970s, neoliberalism emerged, calling for welfare cuts and self-reliance. While this saved money on government balance sheets, it resulted in a skyrocketing wealth gap and left many trapped in the. cycle of working poverty. The third way is social investment. The state invests significant budgets into quality public childcare, which eases the burden on parents, prevents women from being forced to quit their jobs, and allows them to keep working and paying taxes —thereby boosting birth rates and tax revenue simultaneously. Meanwhile, promoting professional retraining and lifelong learning allows part-time workers or the unemployed to upgrade their skills and return to better-paying jobs. Take delivery riders as an example: the traditional " compensate after the fact" mindset. waits for them to slip and break a leg on a rainy day before reviewing a meager compensation payment. But the " social investment" concept means giving them a chance to transition into stable , secure jobs at 25, providing effective career guidance at 40, and offering affordable, reliable childcare when they have kids, so they aren't forced to run deliveries for 14 hours a day. These two approaches might cost a similar amount of budget upfront. The budget may be similar, but 10 years later, the tax contributions and economic output generated for the country will be worlds apart. If a. society only knows how to hand out condolence money after a disaster happens, the number of people falling into the abyss will only grow. In the end, even if you go bankrupt paying out benefits, you will never be able to fill this bottomless pit. In Taiwan, from pension reform and healthcare co-payments to relying on tobacco and estate taxes to support long-term care funds, every adjustment is a tug-of-war of interests between different generations and social classes. The government has been working hard in recent years to promote public childcare subsidies and career guidance.

, trying to shift from a bottomless pit of passive handouts toward social investments that truly create a future. The cost of patching things up after a crisis is always far higher than the cost of supporting people firmly from the start. Fiscal sustainability isn't about everyone tightening their belts; it’s about shifting our perspective on the future and spending money where it truly matters. Now, let’s talk about the bankruptcy of the labor insurance fund. The Ministry of Labor in the ROC pushed through the Labor Occupational Accident Insurance and Protection Act, which officially took. effect on May 1, 2022. This new law allows food delivery riders and casual construction workers to head to a convenience store, tap their iPhones, or use the Bureau of Labor Insurance website to enroll themselves. The numbers certainly show progress; as of mid-2025, the number of people enrolled under this act has surpassed 310,000. But at best, the Act only acts as a bandage after an accident has already occurred. For these laborers, retirement pensions, childbirth benefits, and unemployment relief for. when work dries up remain a legal void. The irony is, even as gig workers struggle to get into the most basic insurance, the safety net covering over 10 million workers across Taiwan is on the verge of collapsing. According to the latest actuarial report released by the Ministry of Labor in early 2025, the government has been dipping into the national treasury since 2020, pouring in nearly 400 billion. Combined with optimistic investment return projections, they've barely managed to delay the fund's bankruptcy from 2028. to 2031. But why is this net tearing? Because the number of retirees drawing from the fund is skyrocketing, while the ultra-low birth rate causes the number of contributors to plummet. In reality, the fund has been running a deficit since 2017, and starting in 2026, its cash flow will turn negative again, leaving less and less in the coffers. The government keeps guaranteeing that labor insurance won’t fail, but the state can't just print money. When subsidies come from general tax revenue, it’s essentially using future taxes to plug a current. black hole, without addressing the root cause: an aging population. The sense of deprivation felt by the younger generation watching this bankruptcy countdown is completely understandable —burdened by high housing prices and low wages, struggling in atypical jobs, and forced to pay out every month. We pay increasingly higher premiums to support the previous generation's retirement, only to realize that 30 or 40 years from now, when it’s our turn , the treasury may long be empty. That is why I must clearly state: if the.

government cannot overhaul the rules with a mindset of social investment, force profitable platform operators to fulfill their social responsibilities, and summon the courage to drive real pension reform, this storm will eventually consume us all. We are not saints; no social safety net can ever be flawless, because every system has its boundaries and every resource has its limits. A safety net that is free, universal, and sustainable all at once cannot exist in reality. What we can decide isn't whether this net has holes. , but where those holes appear, how large they are, and who has the authority to decide these things. So, after hearing all this, what can we actually do? First, if you or your friends are working in gig jobs or freelance, take 10 minutes to check your social insurance status online; don't wait until you're lying in the emergency room to realize there's no net beneath you. Second, next time you see news about pension reform, don't just follow the talk of paying more or getting less; try to look up the. actuarial reports to see the underlying investment returns and demographic projections—often, these are just overly optimistic assumptions that merely delay bankruptcy. Third, when you go to vote, remember to categorize policies into ex-post compensation and ex-ante preparation. Handing out cash is ex-post compensation, while building public childcare, long-term care facilities, and providing solid information are ex-ante preparation. Both are necessary, but how the money is allocated depends on the votes in our hands. This has never been someone else's private business; it’s about. determining whether we can live with dignity when we get old. Finally, a question for everyone to ponder: with the pension fund projected to run dry by 2031, if the government only focuses on paying more, receiving less, or relying on debt to keep it alive, is that intergenerational fairness for today's younger generation facing low wages and high housing prices? Beyond passive financial patching, how should the state introduce the concept of social investment to fundamentally reconstruct this system? And what would you do? We welcome everyone to share your thoughts. Our channel has always. been committed to the ideals of republicanism, hoping to awaken a greater appreciation for democratic values through civic education and historical consciousness. If you enjoyed this episode, don't forget to like, subscribe, and share it with others! You are also welcome to join as a member. See you next time, bye.

值得閱讀的理由

  • 以低生育率與高齡化說明，社會安全網面臨的不只是人口變化，更是財政與制度的考驗。
  • 從世代正義切入退休制度，呈現年輕世代與退休世代之間難以迴避的資源分配問題。
  • 探討非典型勞動者與平台工作者如何落在保障網之外，讓讀者看見勞動型態轉變帶來的風險。
  • 指出福利制度改革不能只轉移帳單，並呼籲以制度改革和公民教育共同打造更公平、可持續的未來。

摘要

社會安全網還撐得住嗎？

阿牛從高房價、低薪與非典型工作者的生活壓力談起，也提醒觀眾，年輕世代如今負擔著逐年增加的保費，支撐上一代退休生活；等到自己三、四十年後老去，國庫是否還有能力承擔，仍是未知數。他指出，若政府無法以社會投資的角度改革制度、要求獲利的平台業者承擔社會責任，並勇於推動真正的退休制度改革，最終可能沒有人能置身事外。

在節目宣傳中，阿牛表示，社會除了需要現金補助，也需要普及的公民教育。系列內容依據教育部一○八課綱的公民與社會領域設計，希望讓基礎公民知識更容易理解，並透過制度改革與公民教育，為重塑社會盡一份心力。接著，他說明本集將討論社會安全網的五項課題：少子化與高齡化、世代公平、非典型勞動、平台經濟，以及財政永續。安全網能否發揮作用，關鍵不只是網有多大，也在於網上有多少破洞。

少子化、高齡化與逐漸變重的負擔

阿牛先以「幾個人撐網、幾個人躺在網上」作比喻：當支撐安全網的人變少、需要依靠它的人變多，網就可能無法承受。國民年金與保險制度多採隨收隨付的方式，也就是由現在的工作者負擔目前退休者的給付，而非每個人都只靠自己的儲蓄。當人口結構從年輕人多、長者少的金字塔，轉為繳費者減少、領取給付者增加的倒金字塔，制度便會承受愈來愈大的壓力。

阿牛引用社會學者阿恩・卡勒伯格對不穩定生活的觀察，指出許多年輕人難以找到穩定工作，也難以規劃人生；買房、結婚與生育等重要選擇只得一再延後。這不是年輕人不夠努力，而是整體結構讓他們進退兩難。學校學生減少、教室合併，甚至校園空間可能改作長者日照用途，也映照出服務對象從孩童轉向長者的人口變化。

戰後嬰兒潮世代陸續退休，使繳納年金與健保的人數逐年減少；另一方面，退休給付、長者醫療資源與長照支出不斷增加。保費負擔愈重，年輕人愈不敢生育，人口與財務壓力也就進一步加劇。阿牛將社會由人口紅利期走向少子高齡期的變化，描述為一個可能持續惡化的惡性循環。

世代契約與公平分擔

阿牛進一步談到世代契約：年輕時照顧上一代，盼望未來由下一代接手照顧自己。然而，這份沒有白紙黑字的契約若失去信任，社會也可能因此分裂。當代享有的福利，有一部分等於預支了未來世代尚未賺取的資源，因此問題不只是要不要照顧長者，更包括由誰承擔成本、如何分配責任。

他援引托馬斯・皮凱提關於資本累積速度快於薪資成長的分析，提出疑問：如果年輕人必須繳更多保費，去支撐資產累積可能已勝過自己的退休世代，這樣的安排是否公平？民主制度也有結構性的時間偏差：現在能投票的人有聲音，尚未出生的世代卻無法參與。以城市預算為例，政府可能選擇立即提高長者福利，而把青年社會住宅延後興建，因為前者今年就能看見成果，後者則須等待多年。

阿牛認為，臺灣退休金改革的爭議，正是世代契約受考驗的表現。改革無法憑空消除成本，往往只是改變由誰付帳；公開精算報告、接受獨立檢視並容許不同意見，才能讓債務與取捨進入公共討論。沒有爭論，不代表問題不存在，代價只是可能以另一種形式到來。

安全網外的非典型勞動者

阿牛接著指出，還有一群人甚至沒有被納入既有的保障計算。他們出現在道路、倉庫與住家門口，卻常常落在安全網之外。臨時工作、自由接案與外送等零工勞動，具有工時不規律、缺少固定雇主等特徵，也往往伴隨保障不足。安全網上的破洞並非偶然，而是制度如何編織、如何界定保障對象的結果。

他引用勞動經濟學者蓋伊・史坦丁對「無產階級化」的描述：這些工作者的生活中缺少對未來的影子。因為無法確定明天是否有工作，今天投入的勞動與作出的承諾便難以轉化為長期保障。與工業時代能以忠誠換取穩定的勞工相比，這群人承受的不只是收入不確定，也包括生活時間感與未來規劃的瓦解。影片字幕在外送員案例尚未說完時中止。

================================================

Every day, we shoulder high housing prices and low wages, struggling in atypical jobs, while being forced to pay ever-increasing premiums each month to support the previous generation's retirement. But thinking about how it will be our turn to grow old in thirty or forty years, the national treasury might be drained by then. Many people actually have two misconceptions about social welfare: one is thinking it's charity given by the government to the disadvantaged; the second is the belief that "as long as I work hard enough, I don't need to rely on the government." But honestly, we must face. reality. The risks in modern society are extremely high and cannot be withstood by individual effort alone. The past model of staying at the same company until retirement is crumbling, and the demographic dividend has disappeared. Therefore, the question now is not whether we need welfare, but how to design a fair and sustainable safety net. Today, we will discuss five concepts regarding the problems appearing in this social safety net: low birth rates and an aging population , intergenerational equity, atypical. labor, the platform economy, and fiscal sustainability. A social safety net is just a net; whether it works well depends not on how big it is, but on the size of its holes. First, let's talk about the low birth rate and aging population that everyone has likely heard discussed for a long time. If this safety net is held by four people with only one person lying in the middle, it’s obviously very stable. But if there are fewer people holding the net and more people lying on it, what happens then? Basically, it just.

can't hold up anymore. That is the challenge we are currently facing: a low birth rate and an aging population. Because our national pension and insurance systems operate on a pay-as-you-go basis; simply put, these are not personal savings accounts, but rather current workers paying to support those currently retired. Once the population pyramid collapses, this support model gets stuck. Sociologist Arne Kalleberg observed in "Precarious Life" that young people today cannot find stable jobs in the labor market and cannot even plan the next stage of. their lives. Buying a house, getting married, and having children—these major life milestones can only be postponed again and again. It’s not that young people aren't working hard; it’s that the entire social structure leaves them in a dilemma. Look at how many elementary schools now have so few students that classrooms are being merged, playgrounds are becoming parking lots, and in a few years, they might even be repurposed as senior day care centers. On the same plot of land, the target demographic has shifted from six-year-olds to eighty-year-olds, and this is the reality we are experiencing . The previous population structure was a pyramid with plenty of young adults, so the net could hold. Now, it has. become an inverted pyramid: fewer people pay premiums, while more seniors collect benefits and use medical resources, creating a vicious cycle. Premiums become heavier, young people become even less daring to have children, and the net sinks even further. This is the dilemma of the low birth rate that Taiwan is currently facing. On one hand, the post-war baby boomer generation is retiring one after another, and the number of people paying into pension and health insurance is decreasing year by year. On the other hand, the total amount of pension payouts, the medical resources consumed by the elderly, and the public. expenditure for promoting Long-Term Care 2.0 are all increasing almost exponentially. The young adults paying into the system are fewer, while the elderly who collect and spend the money are more. This transition can be divided into two periods. The first is the traditional demographic dividend period: high fertility rates, shorter lifespans, and a standard pyramid structure where many young adults support few seniors, resulting in sufficient funds and generous payouts, with a labor market dominated by standard employment and easy entry for youth. The second is the period of an. aging and low-birth-rate society: ultra-low fertility, longer lifespans, and an inverted pyramid where a few young adults support a vast elderly population. Funds face bankruptcy crises, premiums are heavy, service industries and non-standard employment expand, young people face low wages and delayed family formation, and fertility rates fall yet another level. This is a vicious cycle; whether or not we can afford to support those on the margins has never been a moral issue, but an economic and political one. We shouldn't pretend the reality doesn't.

exist, because this web is woven by the choices of our generation. We must face a sharper issue: the so-called intergenerational contract. The hope was that we would care for the older generation when we were young, and the next generation would care for us when we grew old, but once this unsigned contract breaks, social trust vanishes. This web is essentially overdrawing the future; as we lie on it, we are spending money that the next generation has yet to earn. Once this unsigned. intergenerational contract snaps, society will inevitably fracture along with it. The structural issue mentioned by sociologist Thomas Piketty in " Capital in the Twenty-First Century" is quite real: capital accumulates much faster than wages grow. If the system then requires young people to pay higher premiums to support a retired generation that has already accumulated more assets than them, is that fair to the youth? Often, this unfairness stems from the structural blind spots of democracy: those who can vote are present, but those not yet born cannot. vote. When governments choose to prioritize immediate senior welfare payouts over social housing that won't be ready for years, they are effectively pushing the financial burden onto the next generation. For example, imagine a city budget meeting considering two proposals: increasing monthly senior welfare by 1,000 or building new social housing for youth. If the city budget only allows for one, the decision will be to raise the senior payout this year and put off the. housing for two years. Their reasoning is clear: one result is visible this year, the other in four years. This is a common structural bias in democracy —voters are present, while the unborn are absent. The controversy over pension reform in Taiwan is a symptom of this broken contract. It was never really about who owes whom money, but about whose threads should be used to weave this social safety net. We must admit that "reform" alone cannot solve. the problem; it just shifts the bill to someone else. The reason pension equity became a public debate in Taiwan is that someone was willing to publish the actuarial reports and bear the risk of being criticized. In contrast, in a system without independent audits, public reports, or dissent, this debate would never even happen. However, the absence of debate does not mean the debt doesn't exist; it just arrives in a different form. Therefore, it’s not.

really about who owes whom, but whose thread should be used to weave this social safety net; the original way won’t solve the problem, it just changes who pays. This means that because they are unsure if they will. have a job tomorrow, the commitments they make and the labor they put in today have no meaning for the future. Compared to the proletariat of the industrial age who could trade loyalty for security, this "precariat" truly has nothing. It’s not just a matter of income; it’s a collapse of their sense of time. Take a delivery driver, for example; the paper they sign with the platform isn't an employment contract, but a service agreement. What’s the difference? The difference is whether there is anyone to catch you the moment you fall. Economist Kathleen. Thelen, in "Varieties of Liberalization and the New Politics of Social Solidarity," proposes the concept of " dualization," because the current labor market is split in two: "insiders" who enjoy full protection and "outsiders" who are thrown into the market to bear all the risks. The irony is that what determines who you are is not your ability, but where the system draws the line. Suppose a bookstore chain converts all its warehouse staff to temp workers; afterwards, there are two types of people in the same warehouse:. one is the original staff with benefits , annual bonuses, and employer-contributed pensions; the other is the temp staff, doing the exact same work in the exact same spot, yet receiving completely different protections. The most concerning part here isn't actually that the conditions are different, but that although they are in the same space, it is difficult to form a sense of "us." We must acknowledge that those who have fallen through the holes are not outsiders, so whether a contract says "employment" or "service" sometimes determines a.

Businesses use digital technology, networks, and algorithms to create a model that matches labor supply with consumer demand. The convenience it brings is real, but it can also simultaneously upend labor relations and the social safety net. In "The Fissured Workplace," economist David. Weil warns that by outsourcing work, companies are transforming the employer responsibilities they should be carrying into cold, hard commercial contracts. Wages are no longer pay; they are just pricing. Simply put, platforms have become free riders in the welfare system. As sociologist Juliet Schor noted in "After the Gig," platforms shift the costs of worker health and retirement onto society, while maximizing their own profits through an "asset-light" model that avoids ownership as much as possible. Take delivery drivers as an example: the vehicle is theirs and they pay for the gas, but it is that invisible manager—the algorithm—that decides when they stop and how much they earn per order. When issues arise, the platform just says, "We are merely intermediaries; what we signed were service contracts." And just like that, employer liability vanishes into thin air. However, when faced with labor inspections or legal disputes, the platform’s stance shifts to: "Drivers are independent contractors; the platform only manages dispatching and ratings, and does not hold the status of an employer." We can now see that those who manage the most strictly often bear the least responsibility. If this holds. true in reality, it is not because the market is broken, but because the rules were written incorrectly. So, how should we rewrite the rules? When many people hear " fiscal sustainability," they immediately think of cutting spending, slashing budgets, and reducing welfare, but they are completely missing the point. French sociologist Guillaume Morel once proposed a sound principle: preparation beforehand is better than repairs afterward. In other words, rather than waiting for someone to fall from a building half-dead and scrambling to catch them with a net, it is better to build a railing or raise the ground beneath their feet from the very start. When we view social welfare. not as mere consumption, but as an investment that yields returns, the entire calculation changes completely. Looking back at history, traditional post-war Western welfare states favored passive, reactive compensation— providing relief for the unemployed and pensions for the elderly. This worked well in an era of rapid economic growth when the youth population outnumbered the elderly. But by the 1970s, neoliberalism emerged, calling for welfare cuts and self-reliance. While this saved money on government balance sheets, it resulted in a skyrocketing wealth gap and left many trapped in the. cycle of working poverty. The third way is social investment. The state invests significant budgets into quality public childcare, which eases the burden on parents, prevents women from being forced to quit their jobs, and allows them to keep working and paying taxes —thereby boosting birth rates and tax revenue simultaneously. Meanwhile, promoting professional retraining and lifelong learning allows part-time workers or the unemployed to upgrade their skills and return to better-paying jobs. Take delivery riders as an example: the traditional " compensate after the fact" mindset. waits for them to slip and break a leg on a rainy day before reviewing a meager compensation payment. But the " social investment" concept means giving them a chance to transition into stable , secure jobs at 25, providing effective career guidance at 40, and offering affordable, reliable childcare when they have kids, so they aren't forced to run deliveries for 14 hours a day. These two approaches might cost a similar amount of budget upfront. The budget may be similar, but 10 years later, the tax contributions and economic output generated for the country will be worlds apart. , trying to shift from a bottomless pit of passive handouts toward social investments that truly create a future.
